readingInstruction: Read Leviticus 6:1-7:38. These chapters repeat the offerings and add instructions for the priests. They can feel technical, so look for what they tell you about the priests’ role and about the way worshipers were fed and cared for.
settingTheScene: Chapters 1 to 5 were addressed mainly to the people, telling them what to bring. Chapters 6 and 7 are addressed to Aaron and his sons, telling the priests what to do with the offerings. They go over the burnt offering, the grain offering, the sin offering, the guilt offering, and the peace offering again, this time from the priest’s perspective. They show what happens to the meat, who may eat it, and how to guard its holiness.
observation: The fire on the altar “shall not go out” (6:9, 12-13).
The priest wears linen garments to remove the ashes, and then changes clothes to carry them outside the camp (6:10-11).
The grain offering is eaten by the priests, “in a holy place” (6:16-18).
Anything that touches the sin offering becomes holy (6:27).
The guilt offering is “most holy,” and the priest who offers it may eat it (7:1-7).
The priests receive a share of the offerings for their support (7:6-10, 31-36).
The peace offering must be eaten within one or two days, and anyone who eats it while unclean “shall be cut off from his people” (7:15-21).
The fat and blood are forbidden to eat (7:22-27).
interpretation:
The detailed instructions reveal several truths. The first is the unbroken fire. The burnt offering fire on the altar must never go out. It was lit by God himself (Leviticus 9:24), and it was to be kept burning day and night. The priest’s job each morning was to add wood and keep it alive. It is a picture of constant readiness. The way to God is always open, and the place of sacrifice never goes cold.

The second is the care for holiness. The priests change clothes. The ashes are carried to a clean place outside the camp. The utensils that touch the sin offering have to be cleaned or destroyed. The details teach that holy things are not to be treated casually. God’s holiness is not passive. It sanctifies what touches it, and it is dangerous to what is unclean.

The third is the provision for the priests. They receive a share of the offerings as their food. God does not ask them to serve without support. This is an early example of the principle that “those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9:14). It is also a reminder that the people’s offerings feed those who serve them in worship.

The fourth is the careful rules for the peace offering. It must be eaten promptly and in a state of cleanness. A feast with God is not to be taken lightly. To come to the table when unclean is to risk being “cut off.” This will be echoed in the New Testament, where Paul warns about taking the Lord’s Supper “in an unworthy manner” (1 Corinthians 11:27).

Finally, the prohibition on eating blood is repeated, because blood is the life and belongs to God. This is the reason that blood is used for atonement. You will read the explanation in Leviticus 17:11.
connection: Jesus is the priest who offered himself, and he is also the sacrifice that feeds his people. “Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6:54). The fire that never goes out points to the Spirit who has been given to us (Acts 2:3). Paul says that Christians should “present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (Romans 12:1), and Peter says that we are priests who offer “spiritual sacrifices” (1 Peter 2:5).
application:
Ask whether the fire of worship is still burning in your life, or whether it has gone cold.

Think about how you support those who serve you spiritually, such as a pastor, a teacher, or a missionary. Is there a way you could support them more?

Next time you take communion, prepare yourself with care, and approach the table with reverence and gratitude.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to keep the fire of love for him burning in you.
Thank him for feeding his people with himself.
Ask him to teach you to approach his table with reverence.
